title: 8 Things Teachers Do To Encourage Misbehavior https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2010/12/04/8-things-teachers-do-to-encourage-misbehavior/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin identifies eight common, often unconscious teacher behaviors that actively encourage the misbehavior teachers are trying to eliminate: talking over students, rushing around in a hurry, answering call-outs from students who don't raise their hands, moving on with a lesson before students are truly ready, harboring negative thoughts about students, showing irritability, tolerating classroom clutter, and holding a self-defeating belief that students control the class's climate. Each item includes a brief explanation of the mechanism by which it undermines behavior, along with a simple corrective action. The piece frames self-awareness as the first and most important step, arguing that unrecognized habits are the only classroom management problems without a ready solution, and closes by locating the ultimate cause of classroom struggles in the teacher's own mindset and habits rather than external factors.
points: Eight common teacher habits - talking over students, rushing, answering call-outs, moving on too soon, negative thinking, irritability, clutter, and self-defeating beliefs - actively encourage misbehavior.
Talking over students and rushing both create classroom tension that manifests as restlessness and poor listening.
Answering students who call out without raising their hand undermines the credibility of the classroom management plan.
Negative thoughts about students leak out through body language and tone, provoking resentment and worse behavior.
The article locates the root cause of most classroom management struggles in teacher habits, not student character.
quotes: The only classroom management-related problems that don’t have solutions are those we’re unaware of. Once illuminated, there is always a way to solve the problem or make it manageable.
Talking over students breeds inattentiveness, side-talking, and poor listening.
Being in a hurry creates tension in the classroom, causing restlessness, excitability, and poor behavior.
Answering students who don’t raise their hand encourages disrespect and communicates to your students that your classroom management plan is no longer valid.
Negative thoughts about students always bubble to the surface-body language, tone of voice, sarcasm-causing resentment, misbehavior and, ultimately, revenge.
